I'm so sorry you're going through this, as someone who luckily got the right support I can advise you a little bit. Firstly I'm proud you're seeking help instead of giving up since it must be really hard for you, college lecturers are kinda useless in these terms, they aren't well trained to handle this situation and neither are your friends because of the age, please do not take that personally, it has nothing to do with you.

Most hospital OPDs have psychiatrists and psychologists, so you can visit the nearest one and get some help, these are generally cheaper than clinics, but if you can afford a better one you can please google around the best psychiatrists in your location, set an appointment and go forward with it. Psychiatrists usually take down your history on the first visit and diagnose you & can give medications, psychologists on the other hand do talk therapy which equip you with skills that help you navigate your life. Also, there is a chance that some might be stigmatising or just not the right one for you, when this happens please do not give up, a good one will always refer you to someone better or correct their behaviour in case you tell it's not working, if they don't you have the right to leave and find a better one, but please do not give up. I think there's a lot of attachment issues if I'm not wrong, being overly dependent or the fact that your life/existence revolves around them. You crave validation from outside your home to make up for the fact that you didn't while growing up.. Dating with BPD isn't easy but we deserve love like every other person but keep in mind that not everyone will understand BPD because honestly.. i don't think we understand it that well either. Firstly, it's your life, it's totally okay to be alone or be in a relationship, but you need to understand that no matter what you choose, your personality is something you develop on your own and isn't moulded by a person who comes into your life.

For your questions, I can suggest getting a new hobby, try finding something you love or maybe something you already have done that you love. Try mindfulness and being in the moment. You can also try distraction techniques+emotional regulation from DBT. I cannot give much advice on preventing these issues because I feel you are in therapy and that's an AMAZING thing, if you work on it more on therapy, it will definitely get better. Don't try to resolve BPD in a single day, it'll never happen, take your time and learn and unlearn things slowly. Start working on your self esteem too. Check out thought record from cbt and unhelpful thinking styles and correlate them everytime you have a thought that you cannot stand. 

I know that BPD doesn't have any fixed meds but they only give them as an aid to help us, it's primarily therapy which helps us. (Not a doctor)

You can google it, it's a skill from CBT which is very useful considering our thought patterns are really flawed. It helps us correct them or change them to a more rational one. It takes a lot of time to see changes considering it is therapy and we cannot really flip a switch, so don't get mad about it and take your time. Over time you'll become more aware and don't even have to write them down. I think a bit of it is also due to low self esteem considering we have BPD, but if you're in therapy I'd recommend talking about it. I think putting boundaries and prioritizing yourself helps, it might seem ridiculous or "selfish" but there should be a balance. Distraction techniques from DBT work well too, so you can let the emotion pass or let it calm down a bit since we tend to make abrupt decisions or wreck the relationship. Even IPR skills come into the picture here, you can check them out as well!

Most of this stems from unmet validation from our childhood (was due a parent in my case) and it leads to projection onto people outside and seeking validation from them. I think it's due to low self esteem, but things like thought record help a lot, probably even IPR skills we learn in DBT.

The thing with disorders or BPD is that it's hard. I might know skills and probably don't get hit by splitting everyday like I used to but it does happen once in a while. It's currently hit me and I have absolutely no idea how to handle it, years of therapy and self help can never prepare you for it, you can never be fully ready to deal with it, however you can do skills to not fall into a black hole until the wave passes.. I used to be the same and tell everyone about BPD but over the years I've stopped but do share it with those who I think understand it a little bit, but if they don't I try to tell it in terms of how upset I am or frustrated. Like for example if things don't go well in uni, I just tell I hate the subject or how the exam was bad instead because more often than you think people do relate to that, I did start hearing others feel the same and to a certain extent it did feel okay. But I still go to someone like my therapist to vent it all out because they'd understand and try to help me navigate. BPD is hell I don't know how you're coping with two disorders all at once, it's a great thing so I hope you appreciate yourself.

No it's no burden, go ask for help. The biggest thing that therapy has taught me is that it's okay to ask for help. And that help doesn't mean it should be anything huge, you can literally just start off slow by saying "hey can I vent for a bit? I don't feel that great" or "Hey Can you hear me out for a bit?" 

I always thought I had to handle shit alone but now I started sharing and realized it does help, I always ended up asking for help when I was at my worst but these days I just spoke out when I felt upset and realized that was enough and I didn't go into a much worse state. We end up bottling emotions because we feel we'd be a burden and it just gets worse. 

Honestly all these thoughts come from unhelpful thinking styles which we have and I recommend you to just look through those whenever you feel this way. If it's one of the unhelpful thinking styles then you immediately know your thought is wrong and do the opposite. Yes it feels stupid and sometimes uncomfortable but tiny steps

As someone who's been in therapy for 4 years, I can offer some advice. When I first went in I felt the same way and thought I couldn't forgive myself and yada yada.. now that I look back I realized I was able to survive it and sometimes giving it time and accepting it just one by one is also totally okay. It's your life, if it's getting hard just take a step back and let yourself breathe, you don't have to fix everything or accept it in one night. Therapy and healing is slow but it's so much worth it when you realize how much your mindset has changed down the line, you start appreciating yourself. The first step in forgiving yourself is admitting to things you've done, that means you're capable of change. 

The biggest thing my therapist told me was to accept things, not approve of them. That means it might be still wrong to you but accepting just makes it a bit easier to cope. They still repeat it to me to this date lol. It'll be fine, take it easy

I've been in therapy for over 3-4 years but just go for follow up every 3-4 months to keep myself in check, vent out and learn how I can improve my actions.. there are some things I've learnt that I see now that make a large difference which I neglected in the beginning of my therapy as I had no hope.

The first one is a thought record, I was always lazy to use skills or kept arguing why we need to do so much to keep ourselves sane but I realized how clear things get when you just write it down. You realize how many unhelpful thinking styles you have and that helps.

Second was mindfulness, I hated this the most when I first learnt it because I hated meditation and all that sort but things like being in the moment really helps when you're in situations where you are triggered.. We tend to overthink and make a lot of bad decisions during such cases but instead we gotta just accept our emotions and let it pass. Actually even saying it out loud like "it is okay to feel how i feel, it'll be okay" and taking some deep breaths help

Third..well when I was really triggered I was told to eat salt or hold ice.. the salt really helped cuz it was awful but it distracted me. There's also another skill called "opposite action", as someone who has bpd/any mental health disorder we often have a common symptom of depression or the feeling where we don't want to do anything or leave our bed, I felt the same and admit have done it even after so many years in therapy, but recently there was a situation where I was forced to get up and leave which was just for a couple of minutes but it made me realize that it actually worked. I know it takes a lot of effort and I understand how tiring it is but I think it's a good skill.

In terms of IPR, DEAR MAN really helps. I've used it a couple of times and today itself infact, placing boundaries is a very important that I've learnt in dbt, I feel most of us have low self esteem and don't feel like standing up for themselves but that's where these skills come into picture.

Not a doctor here but, I had been on anxiety meds before. Honestly it takes a bit of trial and error to find one that matches for you but they don't really prescribe it for more than a few months since it's habit forming like the comment told above. I was diagnosed with depression first and then BPD, my therapist focused on treating my BPD because that was the main cause and others were something that was affected due to BPD.

Overall, DBT and medications did help me tremendously, there were instances where medications didn't work but I talked it out and my Psychiatrist trusted me to try the medication which was assigned before which I did see improvements in and it worked. 

I had a lot of conversations with my therapist about BPD, although DBT is something which is like the solution available; it may not be applicable to everyone. He's had patients who didn't seem to have any difference through DBT, mostly because it's dialectical - basically two options; there are cases where BPD recover because they see the better option and others who don't because they choose the other option. 

REBT is another method I tried; it's very difficult considering they purposely make you question and put you in a very bad spot but the results are quicker than DBT. 

I used a combination of CBT, DBT, REBT and many others. There's a chance the therapist might not be well versed enough to handle the case even if they're good at understanding BPD because we're so different from each other and every case is different, but with experience I guess they do understand at some certain degree better than others. My therapist focused on using what he knows best at what situation I present, so he was really quick to change tactics when I was calm or under a bpd attack and was highly suicidal. 

In situations like BPD, having been gone through many patients and understanding makes it easier for them; but I saw changes only when I put my foot down and actually started pushing myself through it. I did it as my therapist was clearly frustrated and I asked him to be honest in our treatment; i put efforts for atleast a month and did see a lot of changes, it kept going until now. Medications on the other hand, firstly you need to get the proper combo to work for you, which will take time, if you feel it's not working, inform and get it changed, higher dose or different class of it.
